screening_decisions.reason: This study reports a retrospective analysis of complications after 5,851 consecutive induced first-trimester abortions using bivariable analysis. There is no mention of randomisation or a comparison between different surgical methods. It appears to be an observational cohort study, not an RCT comparing surgical methods.

This is a randomised study of 200 women assigned to conventional vacuum aspiration (VA) or manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) for first-trimester termination (<56 days). It directly compares two different surgical methods in an RCT design, meeting the eligibility criteria.

The study compares mortality and morbidity trends before and after the 1973 Roe v Wade decision. It is not a randomised controlled trial, nor does it compare different surgical methods for first-trimester abortion. It is a population-level temporal analysis.

Although this is a multicentre randomised trial, the comparison is between a prostaglandin vaginal suppository and placebo prior to vacuum aspiration. Both groups undergo the same surgical method (vacuum aspiration); the trial evaluates cervical preparation rather than comparing different surgical methods for termination.

In this study 420 women were randomly assigned to dilatation and curettage (D&C) or vacuum aspiration (VA) for first-trimester abortion. It is an RCT explicitly comparing two different surgical methods, fitting the review objective and selection criteria.

Eighty-four women seeking first-trimester abortion (<10 weeks) were randomised to manual or electric vacuum aspiration. This is an RCT comparing two distinct surgical aspiration methods, making it eligible.

Women requesting first-trimester abortion were randomly assigned to manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) or electric vacuum aspiration (EVA). The abstract explicitly describes random allocation and compares two surgical methods, so it meets the eligibility criteria.

Forty-seven women underwent abortion by vacuum aspiration or classical dilatation and curettage. However, the abstract does not mention randomisation, and the wording suggests a non-randomised comparative or cohort design. Because the selection criteria require RCTs and there is no evidence of random allocation, this study is excluded at title/abstract screening.

This study randomly assigned 300 subjects to metal or flexible plastic cannulae for vacuum aspiration. While it is an RCT, it compares equipment (cannula types) within the same surgical method rather than comparing different surgical methods (e.g., D&C vs VA, or MVA vs VA). Therefore it does not meet the review objective.

One hundred and fourteen women undergoing first-trimester abortion were enrolled in a randomised trial comparing manual vacuum aspiration with electric vacuum curettage. This is an RCT comparing two surgical methods for first-trimester termination and is eligible.
